chapters.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

learn.hook: Why does curd set faster in May than in January? You can find out the way a scientist would: watch, wonder, guess, test and check!
points: Science begins with an observation, something we notice using our senses or instruments, and a question about it.
A hypothesis is a possible answer to the question that can be tested, for example 'Warmth helps milk turn into curd faster.'
We test a hypothesis with an experiment or careful observations, and we record what happens as data, often in a table.
We analyse the data to see if it supports the hypothesis. If it does not, we change the hypothesis and test again. That is not failure, it is learning.
Good scientists repeat their tests, report honestly and share their results so that others can check them.

example.q: Think it through: Aarav says, 'Plants on our balcony grow taller than the plants inside the room because they get more sunlight.' How can he investigate this?
steps: Observation: balcony plants look taller.
Hypothesis: more sunlight makes the plants grow taller.
Experiment: grow two similar pots of the same plant, one in sunlight and one in a dim corner, with the same soil and the same water.
Record the height of each plant every few days in a table.
Analyse: if the sunny plant grows taller, the data supports his hypothesis.
example.answer: He should make a testable hypothesis, run a fair experiment with two similar pots, record heights, and compare the data before concluding.

learn.reallife: Doctors testing a new medicine, farmers trying a new seed variety and ISRO teams testing rocket parts all follow these same steps of investigation.

games.title: Scientist or not?
items: A hypothesis must be something that can be tested.
If there is no way to test an idea, we cannot check whether it is correct.
If the results do not support your hypothesis, the experiment was useless.
Results that disagree with a hypothesis still teach us something and help us form a better hypothesis.
Repeating an experiment makes the results more reliable.
Repeating shows whether the result was a one-time accident or happens every time.
Scientists should change their data if it does not match what they expected.
Data must be reported honestly. Changing data is cheating and misleads everyone.
Observations can be made using our senses or using instruments like a thermometer.
Instruments help us observe and measure things our senses cannot measure exactly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
options: Roses are the most beautiful flowers.
Salt water makes ice melt faster than plain water.
quiz.explain: We can test this by putting the same ice cubes in salt water and plain water and timing them. The other options are opinions that cannot be measured.
steps: A hypothesis must be testable: we must be able to measure or check it
Salt water versus plain water melting ice can be tested by timing identical ice cubes
'Most beautiful', 'fun' and 'boring' are opinions that cannot be measured
Answer: Salt water makes ice melt faster than plain water.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a personal opinion with a testable scientific idea

quiz.q: Meera notices that her bicycle tyre looks flatter in winter. What is this first step called?
quiz.explain: Noticing something with our senses is an observation. Investigations usually start with one.
steps: Meera noticed something using her senses
Noticing with the senses is an observation, the usual first step
A conclusion comes only at the end, after data
Answer: Observation
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of the steps of an investigation

quiz.q: Why should an experiment be repeated several times?
options: To make the result more reliable
So that the hypothesis is always proved right
quiz.explain: Repeating checks that the result was not just luck or a mistake in one trial.
steps: One trial may give a result by luck or by a small mistake
Repeating the test checks this and makes the result more reliable
Answer: To make the result more reliable
quiz.mistake: Thinks repeating an experiment is meant to force a particular answer

quiz.q: Kabir's results do not support his hypothesis. What should he do?
options: Accept the results and think of a new hypothesis to test
quiz.explain: Honest results that disagree with a hypothesis help us improve our idea. Science moves forward this way.
steps: Results that disagree with a hypothesis are still useful
Kabir should report them honestly and test a new hypothesis
Hiding or changing numbers is dishonest and stops learning
Answer: Accept the results and think of a new hypothesis to test
quiz.mistake: Believes an experiment fails if the hypothesis is not supported

quiz.q: What is 'data' in an investigation?
options: The observations and measurements we record
The final opinion of the teacher
The list of materials we buy
quiz.explain: Data are the observations and measurements collected during an investigation, such as heights, times or temperatures.
steps: Data = the observations and measurements recorded during an investigation
e.g. heights, times or temperatures
Answer: The observations and measurements we record
quiz.mistake: Confuses data with the question or the conclusion

quiz.q: Which step comes right after making a hypothesis?
quiz.explain: Once we have a hypothesis, we design and carry out an experiment to test it.
steps: Order: observation and question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion
So after the hypothesis comes testing it with an experiment
Answer: Testing it with an experiment
quiz.mistake: Does not know the order of the steps of an investigation

quiz.q: Why do scientists share their results with others?
options: So others can check and build on the work
So that nobody else ever tests it
Because sharing is a rule only for students
quiz.explain: When others repeat and check the work, mistakes are caught and knowledge grows.
steps: When others repeat and check the work, mistakes are caught
Others can also build on the results
Answer: So others can check and build on the work
quiz.mistake: Thinks science is done in secret by one person

quiz.q: Priya keeps a table of the daily temperature and the time milk takes to set into curd. Which step is she doing?
quiz.explain: Writing measurements in a table is recording data, which she will later analyse.
steps: Priya writes temperatures and setting times in a table
Writing measurements in a table is recording data
Answer: Recording data
quiz.mistake: Mixes up recording data with forming a hypothesis

teach.nudge: But how do I actually find out? What do I do after guessing, and what do I write down?

revise.summary: Science starts with an observation and a question, then a testable hypothesis. We test it with a fair experiment, record data, analyse it, and change the hypothesis if needed, repeating and sharing results honestly.
focus: Order of the steps of an investigation
Telling a testable hypothesis from an opinion
What data is and why tests are repeated
Honest reporting and sharing of results
remember: Observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion
Hypothesis: a possible answer that can be tested
Data: the observations and measurements we record
traps: An opinion like 'roses are most beautiful' is not a testable hypothesis
Results that do not support a hypothesis are not failure — never hide or change them

learn.hook: Two friends race paper boats but one uses a bigger sheet AND blows harder. Who has the better design? Nobody can tell, because two things changed at once!
points: A variable is anything that can change in an experiment, such as temperature, amount of water or type of soil.
The independent variable is the one thing we change on purpose. The dependent variable is what we measure to see the effect.
Controlled variables are all the other things we keep the same so that the test is fair.
In a fair test we change only one variable at a time. Then any difference in results can be linked to that one change.
A control setup is kept without the change, so we can compare the results with it.

example.q: Think it through: Isha wants to know whether warm water makes sugar dissolve faster than cold water. What are her variables?
steps: What does she change on purpose? The temperature of the water, so that is the independent variable.
What does she measure? The time the sugar takes to dissolve, so that is the dependent variable.
What must stay the same? The amount of water, the amount and type of sugar, the glass and how she stirs. These are controlled variables.
example.answer: Independent: water temperature. Dependent: time to dissolve. Controlled: amount of water, amount and type of sugar, stirring and glass.

learn.reallife: When a cricket coach tests a new bat, players use the same ball and pitch so that only the bat is different. That is a fair test!

quiz.q: Rohan tests whether the height of a ramp changes how far a toy car rolls. What is the independent variable?
quiz.explain: Rohan changes the ramp height on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The distance is what he measures.
steps: The independent variable is the one thing changed on purpose
Rohan changes the ramp height
So the ramp height is the independent variable; the distance is measured
Answer: Height of the ramp
quiz.mistake: Confuses the variable that is changed with the one that is measured

quiz.q: In the same ramp test, what is the dependent variable?
quiz.explain: The distance depends on the ramp height, and it is what Rohan measures.
steps: The dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect
Rohan measures how far the car rolls
So it is the distance the car rolls
Answer: Distance the car rolls
quiz.mistake: Picks the changed variable instead of the measured result

quiz.q: Why must we change only one variable at a time?
options: So that we know which change caused the result
So that results are always the same
quiz.explain: If two things change together, we cannot tell which one caused the difference in the results.
steps: If two things change together, we cannot tell which caused the result
Changing one variable at a time links the result to that one change
Answer: So that we know which change caused the result
quiz.mistake: Does not see that changing many things at once mixes up the causes

quiz.q: Neha tests which detergent removes a turmeric stain best. Which should she keep the SAME for every cloth?
options: The size of the stain and the washing time
quiz.explain: To be fair, only the detergent changes. Stain size, cloth, water and washing time must stay the same.
steps: Only the detergent should change
Everything else, like stain size, cloth, water and washing time, must stay the same
These are controlled variables
Answer: The size of the stain and the washing time
quiz.mistake: Thinks the variable being tested should also be kept the same

quiz.q: A student grows one plant with fertiliser and one plant without it. What is the plant without fertiliser called?
quiz.explain: The plant without the change is the control. We compare the fertilised plant with it.
steps: The plant kept without the change (no fertiliser) is used for comparison
A setup kept without the change is the control
Answer: The control
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of a control setup

quiz.q: Which experiment is a fair test of whether sunlight helps seeds sprout?
options: One tray in sunlight with water, one tray in a dark cupboard without water
One tray in sunlight and one in the dark, both with the same water, soil and seeds
Two trays in sunlight with different seeds
One tray in the dark with more seeds
quiz.explain: Only the light is different, so any difference in sprouting can be linked to light.
steps: To test sunlight, only the light should differ
Water, soil and seeds must be the same in both trays
Option with water in only one tray changes two things, so it is unfair
Answer: One tray in sunlight and one in the dark, both with the same water, soil and seeds
quiz.mistake: Misses that water was also changed in the first setup

quiz.q: Anil wants to know if the mass of a pendulum bob affects how long one swing takes. Which is a controlled variable?
quiz.explain: He changes the mass and measures the swing time, so the string length must be kept the same.
steps: Anil changes the mass (independent) and measures the swing time (dependent)
Everything else must stay the same, such as the string length
So string length is a controlled variable
Answer: The length of the string
quiz.mistake: Picks the independent or dependent variable as a controlled one

quiz.q: Why do scientists usually test many seeds instead of just one in each tray?
options: One seed may behave unusually, so more seeds give a reliable result
More seeds make the experiment unfair
It is a rule that only big experiments count
quiz.explain: A single seed might be damaged. Using many seeds gives a result we can trust more.
steps: A single seed may be damaged or behave unusually
Many seeds give a result we can trust more
Answer: One seed may behave unusually, so more seeds give a reliable result
quiz.mistake: Does not understand why a larger sample makes results reliable

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: What makes an experiment a FAIR test? I changed everything at once and got confused!
teach.praise: Oh! Change just one thing, keep the rest the same, and measure the result. Now I can trust my tests!
teach.nudge: How many things should I change at a time? And what happens to all the other things?

revise.summary: In a fair test we change only one variable (independent), measure its effect (dependent) and keep everything else the same (controlled variables). A control setup without the change lets us compare results.
focus: Identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables
Why only one variable is changed at a time
Choosing a fair experiment and using many samples
remember: Independent variable: the one thing we change on purpose
Dependent variable: what we measure to see the effect
Controlled variables: everything else kept the same; control setup: kept without the change
traps: Don't mix up independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables
Don't change two things at once — the test is no longer fair

chapters.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

learn.hook: A single spoonful of garden soil can hold many millions of tiny living things. You just cannot see them without help!
points: Microorganisms (microbes) are living things too small to see with the naked eye. We need a microscope to see most of them.
The main groups are bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses. Many are single-celled; some fungi and algae are many-celled.
Examples: Lactobacillus is a bacterium, yeast and bread mould are fungi, Amoeba and Paramecium are protozoa, and Spirogyra is an alga.
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria. They can multiply only inside the cells of another living thing.
Microbes live almost everywhere: in soil, water, air, inside our bodies, and even in very hot springs and icy places.

example.q: Think it through: Your mother keeps a slice of bread in a warm, damp box for a few days and a fuzzy greyish-green layer appears. Is this a living thing? Which group does it belong to?
steps: The fuzzy layer appeared and grew over days, so it is growing, which living things do.
It needed warmth and moisture, like many microbes.
Fuzzy threads on bread are typical of bread mould, which is a fungus.
example.answer: Yes, it is bread mould, a living fungus. (Mouldy food should not be eaten or sniffed closely.)

learn.reallife: Green slime on a pond or on the walls of a water tank is often algae, and the black spots on old, damp bread are fungi.

learn.hook: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw rows of tiny boxes. He called them 'cells', and biology was never the same again!
points: The cell is the basic unit of life. All living things are made of one cell (unicellular, like Amoeba) or many cells (multicellular, like us).
Robert Hooke named cells in 1665. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using his own lenses, was the first to see living microbes.
Most cells have a cell membrane (outer boundary), cytoplasm (jelly-like filling) and a nucleus (control centre).
Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts (where food is made using sunlight) and usually a large vacuole. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
A light microscope magnifies using two lenses. Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.

example.q: Think it through: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective lens. How many times bigger does a cell look?
steps: Each lens magnifies in turn, so we multiply.
example.answer: 400 times bigger

learn.reallife: Pathology labs use microscopes to look at blood cells when a doctor orders a blood test.

learn.hook: The fluffy idli on your plate, the curd in your raita and the medicine that cured your infection all owe something to microbes!
points: Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk into curd. Yeast and bacteria ferment idli and dosa batter, and the gas they make (carbon dioxide) makes batter and bread dough rise.
Rhizobium bacteria live in the root nodules of pulse plants (legumes) like gram and peas and fix nitrogen from the air, making the soil richer.
Decomposer microbes break down dead plants, animals and kitchen waste into compost (manure), returning nutrients to the soil.
Antibiotics such as penicillin are made from microbes. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from a mould in 1928. Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses.
Harmful microbes (pathogens) cause diseases: typhoid and cholera (bacteria), common cold and flu (viruses), malaria (a protozoan). Some microbes also spoil food.

example.q: Think it through: Why do we keep cooked dal in the refrigerator overnight rather than on the kitchen shelf?
steps: Microbes from the air settle on food and grow on it.
They grow and multiply fastest in warm conditions.
Cold slows their growth, so the dal stays fresh for longer.
example.answer: Low temperature slows the growth of the microbes that spoil food.

learn.reallife: Pickles last for months because salt, oil and spices stop most microbes from growing. Jams use lots of sugar for the same reason.

learn.hook: A cough in one corner of a crowded bus can travel further than you think. How do germs hop from one person to another?
points: Good health means physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.
Communicable (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoa, and can spread from one person to another.
They spread through the air (coughs and sneezes: cold, flu, tuberculosis), through contaminated water or food (cholera, typhoid), through close contact, or through carriers called vectors.
Mosquitoes are common vectors: female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, and Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue and chikungunya.
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and heart disease do not spread from person to person. They are linked to lifestyle, diet, age and family history.

learn.hook: Washing your hands with soap for about 20 seconds is one of the cheapest and most powerful medicines in the world!
points: Wash hands with soap and water before eating, after using the toilet and after playing outdoors.

learn.hook: Your body has its own security force. Vaccines are like a training drill that shows the guards a 'wanted poster' before the real thief arrives!
points: The immune system defends the body. White blood cells fight pathogens and make antibodies that attach to specific germs.
After an infection, the immune system often 'remembers' the germ, so it can fight it faster next time. This is immunity.
A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs, or harmless parts of them. It trains the immune system to make antibodies without causing the disease.
Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796. Thanks to vaccination, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, and India was certified polio-free in 2014.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses. Using them without a doctor's advice or stopping them early helps bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance).

example.q: Think it through: Why does a baby get vaccines even when the baby is perfectly healthy?
steps: Vaccines must act before the germ attacks.

example.answer: Vaccines prevent disease, so they are given before infection, while the child is healthy.

learn.hook: In 1820 a teacher named Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle twitch every time he switched on a current. Electricity was secretly making magnetism!

learn.hook: A giant crane in a scrapyard lifts a whole car with a magnet, then drops it with the flick of a switch. That is an electromagnet at work!
points: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire wound around a soft iron core (like an iron nail). It is a magnet only while current flows.
It becomes stronger with more turns of wire, a larger current (for example, more cells), and an iron core inside the coil.
Reversing the current reverses its north and south poles.
Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed.
Uses: cranes that lift iron scrap, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors and machines that separate iron from waste.

learn.hook: Try walking on a freshly mopped marble floor in socks. Whoosh! You slip because there is too little friction under your feet.
points: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
Rougher surfaces produce more friction. Pressing the surfaces together harder also increases friction.
Friction is useful: it lets us walk, write, hold things and stop a cycle with brakes. Treads on tyres and soles increase grip.
Friction also wears out shoes and machine parts and produces heat. Lubricants (oil, grease), polishing and ball bearings reduce it.
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels help. Air and water also oppose motion (drag), so fast vehicles, birds and fish have streamlined shapes.

example.q: Think it through: A heavy box of books is hard to push across the floor. How can you move it more easily?

learn.hook: An astronaut weighing 600 newtons on Earth would weigh only about 100 newtons on the Moon, yet she would still have exactly the same amount of 'stuff' in her body!
points: Gravity is the force with which the Earth pulls every object towards its centre. Every object with mass attracts others, but the Earth's pull is what we notice.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) and stays the same everywhere.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object. Since it is a force, it is measured in newtons (N), using a spring balance.
On Earth, weight (in N) ≈ mass (in kg) × 9.8. So a 1 kg bag of rice weighs about 9.8 N.
The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so an object weighs about one-sixth as much on the Moon, while its mass does not change.

points: Pressure is the force acting on a unit area: pressure = force ÷ area. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa); 1 Pa = 1 N per square metre.
The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure. That is why knives are sharp and nails are pointed, while school bags have wide straps.
Liquids press on the bottom and sides of their containers. Liquid pressure increases with depth, so water spurts farthest from the lowest hole in a bottle.
Air also has weight and presses on everything in all directions. This is atmospheric pressure; at sea level it is about 1,01,325 Pa (roughly 1 lakh pascal).
Air pressure decreases as we go higher, which is why ears may 'pop' on a drive up to the hills or in an aeroplane.

learn.hook: On a hot afternoon at Marina Beach in Chennai, a cool breeze blows in from the sea. By night it turns around. Why does the wind change sides?
points: Wind is moving air. Air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure. The bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind.
Warm air expands, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler air moves in to take its place. This creates wind.
Land heats up and cools down faster than water. By day, land is warmer, so a sea breeze blows from sea to land. By night, land is cooler, so a land breeze blows from land to sea.

Uneven heating on a huge scale drives the monsoon. In summer the land of India becomes very hot, and moist winds from the oceans blow in and bring the rains (the south-west monsoon, mainly June to September).
Fast-moving air has lower pressure. Strong winds over a roof can lower the pressure above it so that a weak roof may lift off.

example.q: Think it through: You hold a strip of paper below your lips and blow over its top. The strip rises. Why?

example.answer: The pressure above the strip is lowered by the fast-moving air, so the higher pressure below pushes it up.

learn.hook: Weather scientists can now spot a cyclone days before it reaches the coast. Their warnings help millions of people get to safety in time!
points: Thunderstorms often form on hot, humid days when warm, moist air rises quickly, forms tall clouds and brings lightning, thunder, strong winds and heavy rain.
A cyclone forms over warm ocean water. Moist air rises, creating a region of very low pressure, and winds spiral in around it at high speed. The calm centre is called the eye.
The same kind of storm is called a hurricane near the Americas and a typhoon in the western Pacific. In India, more cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal than in the Arabian Sea.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) tracks cyclones with satellites and radar and issues warnings. Coastal states run cyclone shelters and evacuation plans.

Cyclone safety: follow official warnings, keep an emergency kit (water, dry food, torch, first-aid, charged phone, documents), move to a shelter if told, stay indoors, keep away from fallen wires, and fishermen should not go to sea.

example.answer: No. Move into a building quickly. If you cannot, crouch low in the open, away from tall trees and poles.

topics.title: Matter is made of tiny particles

learn.hook: Light an agarbatti in one corner of the room and soon the whole room smells of it. The smell travels without anyone carrying it. How?
points: All matter is made of extremely tiny particles, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.
There are spaces between particles. When sugar dissolves in water, its particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Particles are always moving. When particles of one substance spread out and mix with another by themselves, it is called diffusion.
Diffusion is faster when the temperature is higher, because heated particles move faster. Diffusion is fastest in gases and slowest in solids.
Particles attract each other. This force of attraction holds them together; it is strongest in solids and weakest in gases.

example.q: Think it through: A drop of ink is gently added to a glass of hot water and another to a glass of cold water. In which glass does the colour spread through faster, and why?
steps: The colour spreads because ink particles and water particles keep moving and mixing: diffusion.
Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster.
Faster particles mix sooner.
example.answer: In the hot water, because its particles move faster and diffusion happens more quickly.

topics.title: Solids, liquids, gases and the spaces between particles

learn.hook: Why can a lot of CNG be squeezed into the small cylinder of an auto-rickshaw, but you cannot squeeze a brick even a little?
points: Solids: particles are very closely packed with very little space between them and strong attraction. They only vibrate in place, so solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
Liquids: particles are a little farther apart with weaker attraction. They can slide past each other, so liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container.
Gases: particles are far apart with very weak attraction and move freely in all directions. Gases have no fixed shape or volume and fill any container.
Because gas particles have large spaces between them, gases can be compressed a lot. Solids and liquids can hardly be compressed.
Changing the state of a substance (like ice to water) changes the arrangement and spacing of its particles, not the particles themselves.

example.q: Think it through: You press the plunger of a sealed syringe filled with air, then one filled with water. What happens and why? (Do not point a syringe at anyone.)
steps: Air particles have large spaces between them.
Pressing pushes air particles closer, so the plunger moves in a lot.
Water particles are already close together, so the plunger hardly moves.
example.answer: The air syringe compresses easily but the water syringe hardly at all, because gas particles have much more space between them.

learn.hook: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool on a hot summer day, even without a fridge?
points: Heating gives particles energy. At the melting point a solid turns into a liquid; ice melts at 0 °C.
At the boiling point a liquid turns into a gas throughout its volume. Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, at temperatures below boiling. It is faster when it is hot, windy, dry, and when the surface area is larger.
Evaporation causes cooling: the faster-moving particles escape and take energy away. Sweating and the clay matka both cool this way.
Condensation is gas turning into liquid, as on the outside of a cold glass. Some solids, like camphor and naphthalene balls, change directly into vapour; this is sublimation.

chapters.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

learn.hook: Everything around you, from your pencil to the Taj Mahal, is built from just 118 known 'ingredients' called elements!
points: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical methods.
118 elements are known today. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, iron, copper, gold and sulfur.
Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, the first always a capital: H (hydrogen), O (oxygen), C (carbon), N (nitrogen), Fe (iron), Cu (copper), Na (sodium), Au (gold), Ag (silver).
Most elements are metals. Metals are usually shiny, can be beaten into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), and conduct heat and electricity well.
Non-metals such as sulfur, carbon and oxygen are usually dull and brittle when solid, and are poor conductors. (Graphite, a form of carbon, is an exception: it conducts electricity.)

learn.hook: Hydrogen is a gas that burns. Oxygen helps things burn. Join them chemically and you get water, which puts out fires! How can that be?
points: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion.
A compound has properties different from the elements it is made of. Sodium (a very reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) form common salt, which we eat.
Every compound has a fixed composition and a formula: water is H₂O (2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom), carbon dioxide is CO₂, common salt is NaCl.
A compound can be split into its elements only by chemical methods, not by simple physical methods like filtering or using a magnet.
Energy (like heat or light) is often taken in or given out when a compound is formed.

example.q: Think it through: Iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed. A magnet pulls out the iron. After the mixture is strongly heated in a lab, the new black solid is no longer attracted by the magnet. What happened?
steps: Before heating, iron kept its own property of being attracted to a magnet: it was a mixture.
Heating made iron and sulfur combine chemically.
The new substance, iron sulfide, has new properties, so the magnet cannot pull out the iron.
example.answer: A compound (iron sulfide) was formed, with properties different from iron and sulfur. (This is a lab demonstration only.)

learn.hook: A plate of chivda has poha, peanuts, curry leaves and raisins. You can pick out each one. That is the secret of a mixture!
points: A mixture contains two or more substances mixed physically in any proportion. Each substance keeps its own properties.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods: handpicking, sieving, using a magnet, decanting, filtration and evaporation.
A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout, like salt dissolved in water, air, or brass. A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform, like sand in water or oil on water.
Alloys are mixtures of a metal with other elements: brass is copper and zinc; steel is mainly iron with a little carbon.
Elements and compounds are pure substances: they have a fixed composition. Mixtures are not pure substances.

chapters.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

learn.hook: Stir sugar into nimbu pani and it vanishes. But taste it and the sweetness is everywhere! Where did the sugar go?
points: When a substance dissolves, it spreads evenly through another substance, forming a solution. A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
The substance that dissolves is the solute (sugar). The substance in which it dissolves is the solvent (water).
Mass is not lost when something dissolves: mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.
Substances that dissolve in a solvent are soluble (salt, sugar in water). Those that do not are insoluble (sand, chalk powder in water).

Water dissolves so many substances that it is called the universal solvent. Other solvents exist too: nail-polish remover dissolves nail paint, and turpentine dissolves oil paint. Solutions can also hold gases, like carbon dioxide in soda water.

learn.hook: Keep adding sugar to a glass of cold water and a point comes when no more will dissolve. Warm it, and suddenly it can take in more. Why?
points: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a fixed amount of solvent at a given temperature.
A solution in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature is saturated. If more can still dissolve, it is unsaturated.
For most solids, like sugar, solubility increases when the temperature rises. That is how sugar syrup for gulab jamun is made with hot water.
Gases are less soluble in warm water than in cold water. A warm soda bottle fizzes more when opened, and warm water holds less oxygen for fish.
Stirring and powdering make a solute dissolve faster, but they do not change how much can dissolve (the solubility).

example.q: Think it through: Sugar stops dissolving in a cup of water at room temperature. Riya warms the cup gently and the leftover sugar dissolves. What does this show?
steps: Sugar stopped dissolving, so the solution was saturated at room temperature.
After warming, more sugar dissolved.
So the solubility of sugar increased with temperature.
example.answer: The solubility of sugar increases with temperature; the warm solution can hold more sugar.

topics.title: Reflection and images in a plane mirror

learn.hook: Why is the word AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance? A mirror holds the answer!
points: When light falls on a shiny surface and bounces back, it is called reflection. The ray hitting the mirror is the incident ray; the ray bouncing off is the reflected ray.
The normal is a line drawn at 90° to the mirror where the ray strikes it. Angles are measured from the normal.
Law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
A plane mirror forms an image that is erect (upright), the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
The image is virtual (it cannot be caught on a screen) and laterally inverted: left and right appear swapped.

example.q: Think it through: A ray of light makes an angle of 30° with the surface of a plane mirror. What is the angle of reflection?
steps: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror.
Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60°.
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 60°.

topics.title: Lenses and the images they form

learn.hook: Your grandparents' reading glasses, a phone camera and a school microscope all work because of a curved piece of glass called a lens!
points: A lens is a piece of transparent material with at least one curved surface. Light bends (refracts) as it passes through it.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It brings parallel rays of light together (converging lens).
A convex lens held close to an object gives an enlarged, erect, virtual image: this is a magnifying glass. For a distant object, it forms a real, inverted image on a screen.
A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It spreads light rays apart (diverging lens) and always forms an erect, smaller, virtual image.
Lenses are used in spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and projectors. Safety: never look at the Sun through a lens, and never use a lens to focus sunlight on anything, as it can burn.

example.q: Think it through: Anjali holds a lens between a bright window and a white wall and sees a small, upside-down picture of the window on the wall. Which lens is it?
steps: The image is caught on the wall, so it is a real image.
It is inverted, which happens for a real image from a convex lens.
A concave lens always gives virtual images, which cannot be caught on a wall.
example.answer: A convex lens.

topics.title: Day, month and year from the sky

learn.hook: Long before clocks and phones, people knew when to sow seeds and when to celebrate harvests just by watching the Sun, the Moon and the stars!
points: A day comes from the Earth spinning on its axis (rotation). From one sunrise to the next takes about 24 hours.
A month comes from the Moon's phases. From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
A year comes from the Earth going once around the Sun (revolution). It takes about 365¼ days, so every fourth year gets an extra day, 29 February: a leap year.
Through the year the Sun's rising point on the horizon slowly shifts north and south, and the length of shadows at noon changes. People used sticks (gnomons) and sundials to track this.

In the northern half of the Earth, the longest day comes around 21 June (summer solstice) and the shortest around 22 December (winter solstice). Around 21 March and 23 September (equinoxes), day and night are nearly equal.

example.q: Think it through: A calendar year has 365 days, but the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go around the Sun. What would happen if we never added leap days?
steps: Each year the calendar would fall about ¼ day behind the Earth's actual position.
After 4 years that adds up to about 1 day.
Over a few centuries the dates would drift by weeks, and seasons would arrive in the 'wrong' months.
example.answer: The calendar would slowly drift away from the seasons, so we add a leap day roughly every four years.

learn.hook: The Moon seems to grow from a thin silver smile into a full round plate and then shrink away again. But it never really changes shape!
points: The Moon has no light of its own. It shines because it reflects sunlight, and the half facing the Sun is always lit.
As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half. These changing shapes are called phases.

Order of phases: new moon (Amavasya, Moon not visible), waxing crescent, first quarter (half moon), waxing gibbous, full moon (Purnima), waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent, and back to new moon.
The bright part grows (waxes) for about 15 days from new moon to full moon, called Shukla Paksha in many Indian calendars, and shrinks (wanes) for about 15 days, called Krishna Paksha.
The full cycle takes about 29.5 days. The Moon also rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average; a full moon rises around sunset.

learn.hook: Why does a festival fall in October one year and November the next, while your birthday stays on the same date every year? Different calendars!
points: A solar calendar follows the Sun and the seasons. The Gregorian calendar we use for school and work is solar, with 365 days and 366 in a leap year.
A lunar calendar follows the Moon. Twelve lunar months of about 29.5 days make about 354 days, roughly 11 days shorter than a solar year.
So in a purely lunar calendar, dates slowly shift through the seasons. The Hijri calendar is an example of a lunar calendar.

A lunisolar calendar uses lunar months but adds an extra month about every two and a half to three years to keep in step with the seasons. Many traditional Indian calendars do this; the extra month is called Adhik Maas.
India's national calendar, the Saka calendar, was adopted in 1957. Its first month, Chaitra, usually begins on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

learn.hook: A small village pond has fish, frogs, water lilies, dragonflies, sunlight, mud and water, all working together like one big team!
points: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with the non-living things around them.
Living (biotic) parts include plants, animals and microorganisms. Non-living (abiotic) parts include sunlight, air, water, soil, minerals and temperature.
Ecosystems can be large or small: a forest, a grassland, a desert, a pond, a sea, or even a rotting log.
India has many ecosystems: the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, the rainforests of the Western Ghats, the Thar Desert and Chilika Lake in Odisha.
The living things in an ecosystem are suited (adapted) to its non-living conditions, like camels to the hot, dry desert.

example.q: Think it through: In a school garden there are neem trees, earthworms, sparrows, soil, sunlight and rainwater. Sort them into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
steps: Living things grow, need food and reproduce: neem trees, earthworms and sparrows.
Non-living parts do not do these things: soil, sunlight and rainwater.
Together, and interacting, they form the garden ecosystem.
example.answer: Living: neem trees, earthworms, sparrows. Non-living: soil, sunlight, rainwater.

learn.hook: The energy in the muscles of a tiger chasing a deer in Kanha started out as sunlight falling on a blade of grass!
points: Green plants are producers: they make their own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (photosynthesis).
Consumers eat other living things. Herbivores eat plants (deer), carnivores eat animals (tiger), and omnivores eat both (bear, crow, humans).
A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows pointing towards the eater: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.
Energy passes along the chain, but much of it is used for living and lost as heat at each step. Only a small part (about 10%) passes to the next level, so food chains are usually short.
In nature, food chains link together to form a food web. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead remains at every level and return nutrients to the soil.

example.q: Think it through: In the chain grass → deer → tiger, which is the producer, which is the herbivore and which is the carnivore? Where does the energy begin?
steps: Grass makes its own food using sunlight: producer.
The deer eats grass: herbivore (primary consumer).
The tiger eats deer: carnivore (secondary consumer).
The energy begins with sunlight captured by the grass.
example.answer: Grass is the producer, deer the herbivore and tiger the carnivore; the energy comes from the Sun.

learn.hook: No bees, no mangoes? It is true! Many fruit trees need bees and other insects to carry pollen from flower to flower.
points: Living things depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. This is called interdependence.
Plants give oxygen and food; animals breathe out carbon dioxide that plants use. Bees and butterflies pollinate flowers, and birds and animals spread seeds.

If one population changes, others are affected. If frogs disappear from a field, insects may increase while snakes that eat frogs may decrease.
A balanced ecosystem has many kinds of living things. Human activities like cutting forests, pollution and overfishing can upset this balance.

topics.title: What makes life possible on Earth

learn.hook: Venus is hotter than an oven and Mars is a freezing desert. Earth, the third planet from the Sun, is 'just right'. Out of all the planets we know, only Earth is known to have life!
points: Earth is at a suitable distance from the Sun, so it is neither too hot nor too cold, and water can stay liquid on its surface.
Liquid water covers about 71% of Earth's surface. All living things need water. But about 97% of Earth's water is salty sea water, and most fresh water is frozen as ice.
Earth's atmosphere gives us oxygen to breathe and carbon dioxide for plants. It also traps some heat, keeping Earth's average temperature comfortable, about 15 °C.
The ozone layer high in the atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays.
Earth also has fertile soil for plants, and a magnetic field that helps shield it from harmful particles streaming from the Sun.

example.q: Think it through: Why is liquid water so important when scientists search for life on other planets?
steps: Every living thing on Earth needs water to survive.
Water dissolves nutrients and carries them in living bodies.
So a planet with liquid water is more likely to support life as we know it.
example.answer: All known life needs liquid water, so it is one of the first things scientists look for.

topics.title: Our air and the ozone shield

learn.hook: Every breath you take is a mixture of gases, and only about one-fifth of it is the oxygen your body needs!
points: Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, about 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases such as argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Oxygen is used by most living things to get energy from food. Carbon dioxide, though only about 0.04% of air, is used by plants to make food.
Some gases, like carbon dioxide and methane, trap heat. This natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm, but adding too much of these gases is warming Earth more and changing the climate.

The ozone layer can be damaged by chemicals called CFCs, once used in old refrigerators and sprays. Countries agreed in the Montreal Protocol (1987) to phase them out, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
Burning fuels, smoke from vehicles and burning waste pollute the air and can harm our lungs. Clean air is essential for good health.

example.q: Think it through: If air contains about 21% oxygen, how many litres of oxygen are in 100 litres of air?
steps: 21% means 21 parts out of 100.
21% of 100 litres = 21 litres.
example.answer: About 21 litres

learn.hook: There is no Planet B! But small daily choices, like carrying a cloth bag, can add up to a big difference for Earth.
points: Earth faces problems like air and water pollution, plastic waste, cutting of forests, loss of wild species and climate change.
Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place. Protecting it keeps ecosystems healthy and balanced.
India protects wildlife through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves. Project Tiger, started in 1973, helped protect tigers and their forests.
Communities have also protected nature. In the Chipko movement of the 1970s in the Himalayan region, villagers hugged trees to stop them from being cut.
We can help by following the 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; by saving water and electricity, segregating wet and dry waste, planting native trees, and using public transport or cycling.
